prompt:
Create exactly ONE new file:
  1. deploy/restore-drill.sh

A backup nobody has restored is a hypothesis. This restores the most recent dump into a scratch
database, proves it came back, and drops it. Read deploy/backup-fedbench.sh and
deploy/verify-endpoint.sh first and follow their shape: assertions block, --check that changes
nothing, numbered steps, an undo note.

THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT DETAIL: pass --exit-on-error to pg_restore. It is NOT the default.
Without it pg_restore prints "WARNING: errors ignored on restore: N" and EXITS 0, so any scheduled
check of the exit status certifies a half-restored database forever. Say that in a comment where
somebody editing the line will read it.

What it does:
* Picks the newest *.dump in the backup directory unless --dump is given; report which and its age.
  A drill that silently tests a stale dump proves nothing about last night's.
* Creates a scratch database with a name that cannot collide with a real one, restores into it with
  --exit-on-error, then RUNS COUNTS and compares them against the LIVE database rather than against
  numbers hardcoded in the script. Hardcoded expectations rot; a comparison against the source is
  still true next year. Use seeded tables that are never legitimately empty.
* Treats a zero count as a FAILURE even when the restore exited 0 -- schema without rows is the
  shape this whole system's RLS design can produce elsewhere, and a backup is the worst place to
  discover it.
* Also verifies the .sql.gz twin for the same day: `gzip -t` at minimum, and confirm it contains
  actual COPY/INSERT data rather than only DDL.
* ALWAYS drops the scratch database, including on failure. A drill that leaves debris is a drill
  people stop running. Use a trap.
* Refuses outright to touch the real fedbench database. Make that structural, not a convention:
  the scratch name is constructed and checked, and the script exits if it ever resolves to fedbench.
* Prints a one-line verdict and exits non-zero on any failure.

Do not write a systemd unit or timer; that is a separate change.

LIVE ON edaserver, verified 2026-09-14:
  https://edaserver.tailcb2a72.ts.net — Caddy on 443 bound to the tailnet addresses only.
    /rest/v1/*, /storage/v1/* -> nginx shim 127.0.0.1:8087 -> PostgREST :3000 / fed_storage :3001
    /api/*, /healthz          -> vault-api 127.0.0.1:8099 (vaultsvc)
  /healthz -> {"ok":true,"checks":{"database":{"ok":true,"field_definitions":32}}}
  Database fedbench, 19 migrations. connect.health is all zeros -- the schema is built, no vault
  DATA has been migrated from hosted Supabase yet. Seeded counts that ARE non-zero and are the
  useful fixtures: vault.field_definitions 32, vault.option_values 77, vault.measurement_kinds 7,
  vault.metric_definitions 11.

BACKUPS, as of today:
  deploy/backup-fedbench.sh runs nightly at 02:20 via fedbench-backup.timer, as the postgres user
  (a superuser over peer auth -- it must bypass RLS, because every vault table has RLS enabled with
  no policies and pg_dump runs with row_security=off).
  It writes BOTH a custom-format archive and a .sql.gz plain twin into /srv/fedbench/backups
  (postgres:postgres 0700, parent /srv/fedbench root:root 0755 because it is shared with fedbackup).
  First successful run produced fedbench-2026-09-14.dump (186K) and .sql.gz (32K).
  psql and pg_dump live under /usr/pgsql-17/bin/. A bare `psql` resolves to Siemens Calibre's.

SHELL RULES for this box, learned the hard way:
  LF only; a CR breaks bash at the first `for ... ; do`, and systemd does not strip one from a unit.
  Never a literal backslash-n where a line continuation belongs -- bash reads it as an escaped `n`.
  `set -uo pipefail`, never `set -e`: a failed check must be REPORTED, not abort the run half way.
  A pipeline's exit status belongs to the LAST command; `cmd | tail` hides cmd's failure.
  Define every helper you call (ok/bad/warn/step) -- bash resolves the name at RUN time, so calling
    an undefined one prints "command not found", loses the message, and does not change the exit
    status. tests/deployScripts.test.ts fails the build on that, on CRs, and on control bytes.
  Assert CAPABILITY, never existence. Three failures today were existence checked and capability
    not: an OS account that existed with no database privileges; a unit file that existed pointing
    somewhere unexecutable; a directory that existed under a parent its user could not traverse.

HOUSE STYLE, not optional:
* Explain WHY. Every non-obvious line says what breaks if it is wrong and names the MISLEADING
  symptom it produces.
* No marketing tone, no adjective lists, no emoji.
* Invent nothing you cannot verify from files in this worktree; say so in your summary instead.
* If a property you are asked to pin is genuinely violated by the tree, do NOT weaken the check and
  do NOT edit the file under test. Leave it failing and say so.
* End by reporting what you changed AND what you deliberately did not change, and why.

Create exactly ONE new file:
  1. tests/restoreDrill.test.ts

A vitest suite over deploy/restore-drill.sh (written in the same batch as this test -- read it from
the worktree). Match the style of tests/backupScript.test.ts and tests/applyMigrations.test.ts.

Pin the properties that make the drill meaningful rather than decorative:

1. `--exit-on-error` IS PASSED TO pg_restore. Without it pg_restore prints "WARNING: errors ignored
   on restore: N" and exits 0, so the drill would certify a half-restored database forever. This is
   the single assertion most worth having.
2. It NEVER drops or restores over the real database. Assert the script cannot issue dropdb/restore
   against `fedbench` itself -- there must be a guard, not just a differently-named variable.
3. It compares counts against the LIVE database rather than hardcoded numbers. Hardcoded
   expectations rot silently; assert the script queries the source for its expectations.
4. A zero row count fails the drill even when the restore succeeded.
5. The scratch database is dropped on FAILURE as well as success -- assert a trap or equivalent.
6. Absolute /usr/pgsql-17/bin paths, not bare pg_restore/psql.

Assert the script exists and exceeds a minimum length in its own `it`; every check above is a text
search, and a text search over a missing file passes while verifying nothing.

Include an `it` proving the --exit-on-error detector fires against an inline string that calls
pg_restore WITHOUT it.

If the script genuinely violates one of these, leave the assertion failing and say so.

Edit exactly ONE file:
  1. docs/ENDPOINT_RUNBOOK.md

Add a backups-and-restore section. Read deploy/backup-fedbench.sh, deploy/backup-install.sh and
deploy/fedbench-backup.service first.

Cover:
* What runs, when, as whom, and where it writes. Say WHY it runs as postgres rather than fedbackup:
  fedbackup has no privileges inside the database at all, and the dump must be made by a role that
  bypasses RLS, because every vault table has RLS enabled with no policies and pg_dump runs with
  row_security=off.
* Why BOTH formats are kept: a -Fc archive needs a matching-or-newer pg_restore forever, while a
  .sql.gz is readable by zgrep, by a human, and by any future Postgres.
* That these are LOCAL dumps on the database's own host: not an off-host copy, not a second
  physical copy, and they do not clear the cutover gate. The hosted Supabase projects are the only
  off-host copy until cutover, and after cutover they are not one either.
* How to check the backup actually ran, and that a fixed unit does not clear a previous failed
  state -- the next successful run does, or `systemctl reset-failed`.
* A symptom table entry for each real failure seen on 2026-09-14:
    status=203/EXEC -> systemd could not EXEC the script (not "the script errored"); the unit
      pointed into a service account's home, which is user_home_t and cannot be exec'd.
    exit 1, ~5ms, no output -> the service user could not traverse the parent of the backup
      directory. `namei -l <dir>` shows the whole path's modes and is the fastest diagnosis.
    "permission denied for schema vault" -> the dump is being made by a role with no privileges.
* Say plainly that the backup failed three nights running before anyone noticed, and that nothing
  currently alerts on it. Do not soften that; it is the open risk.
